title: Psalm 6: How Long, Lord?
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro
summary: This sermon explores Psalm 6 as David's prayer for God's mercy in the midst of sin and discipline. Pastor Lyro examines how believers struggle with sin and conviction, emphasizing that God's discipline comes from love and always aims at repentance and sanctification. The message concludes with three practical applications: running to Christ when sin condemns you, bringing your deepest sorrows to Jesus, and waiting patiently for God's sanctifying work.

outline.title: The Reality of Sin's Struggle in the Christian Life
subpoints: Sin destroys people, families, and churches; it grieves God and required Christ's death to eliminate eternal consequences
God chose not to eliminate temporal struggles with sin because sanctification through struggle brings greater glory to God
Many seasons of Christian life feel devoid of grace, where prayers seem unanswered and God feels distant
Even the Apostle Paul experienced overwhelming struggle with sin, crying 'O wretched man that I am'
The only solution is to throw ourselves upon the mercies of God through Jesus Christ

outline.title: Understanding Psalm 6: A Prayer for Mercy in Discipline
subpoints: Psalm 6 is a song prescribed for worship, set to stringed instruments in octave (bass voices), matching the sorrowful tone
David's sin caused him to experience God's chastening, designed to drive him to repentance
God disciplines believers (not punishes them) as a means to a greater end: repentance and conformity to Christ
David does not ask God to remove discipline, only to apply it with mercy rather than wrath
God's chastening demonstrates His love; the absence of discipline would mean God doesn't care

outline.title: David's Appeal Based on God's Character, Not His Own Merit
subpoints: David pleads for grace he doesn't deserve, acknowledging he warrants God's wrath
David comes empty-handed, recognizing God as a God of grace, mercy, and covenant
Living in sin annihilates confidence and assurance in God's love
Those who know God will keep His commandments; those who claim to know Him but disobey are liars
David cannot bear the prospect of God's displeasure and asks 'how long' will this last

outline.title: The Answer to 'How Long': God Never Forgets His People
subpoints: God's answer to 'how long' is always 'as long as it takes' to drive you to Jesus Christ
God never forgets His people; this is more certain than a mother's love for her child
Examples like Joseph, David, and Paul seemed forgotten for years while God was building godly character
There is no such thing as instant godliness; maturity requires time and trials
The most prevalent command in Psalms is 'wait'—an active waiting and faith in the Lord
Jesus dwells at the end of our rope, when we have exhausted all human efforts

outline.title: David's Crisis of Assurance and the Possibility of Judgment
subpoints: Verse 5 is the most difficult verse: 'For in death there is no remembrance of you, in the grave, who will give you thanks'
David expresses doubt about his salvation, fearing hell or the place of the dead
His anguish is shown through extreme weeping: his bed drowns in tears, his eyes waste away with grief
This crisis occurs because David had lost assurance of his standing with God through sin
When living is Christ, dying is gain; when living is not Christ, there is no confidence in the afterlife

outline.title: Deliverance and the Transformation from Despair to Hope
subpoints: God answered David's prayer, causing a sudden shift in mood from despair to confidence
David declares separation from workers of iniquity, recognizing God has heard his weeping and supplication
David prays for the repentance of his enemies—those with whom he was sinning—desiring their salvation
This demonstrates David's transformation through his own discipline: he wants others to experience God's sanctifying work
The psalm ends with a prayer for repentance rather than judgment

outline.title: Living Out Psalm 6 in Light of the Gospel: Three Practical Applications
subpoints: Run to Christ when your sin condemns you—Christ bore the wrath our sins deserve so believers never face judicial condemnation
The Father disciplines believers as beloved children, not as condemned criminals, because Christ has already paid the curse
Bring your deepest sorrows to Jesus; He is the man of sorrows who wept and agonized, understanding repentant sinners
Christ never casts out those who confess their sins and seek His mercy; He ever lives to intercede for His people
Wait patiently for God's sanctifying work; our standing with God rests on Christ's finished work, not the speed of our sanctification
One day the struggle with sin will end forever when we are glorified in Christ's presence

transcript:
## Scripture Reading: Psalm 6

> To the chief musician with stringed instruments, on an eight stringed harp, a Psalm of David.
>
> O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor chasten me in your hot displeasure. Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak. O Lord, heal me, for my bones are troubled. My soul also is greatly troubled, but you, O Lord, how long? Return, O Lord, deliver me. O save me for your mercy's sake. For in death there is no remembrance of you, in the grave, who will give you thanks? I am weary with my groaning. All night I make my bed swim. I drench my couch with tears. My eyes waste away because of grief. It grows old because of all my enemies. Depart from me, O you workers of iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping. The Lord has heard my supplication. The Lord will receive my prayer, that all my enemies be ashamed and greatly troubled. Let them turn back and be ashamed suddenly. (Psalm 6)

---

## The Seriousness of Sin and God's Redemptive Purpose

We often joke about sin and we joke about things that are wrong. Yet sin is an awful thing. It destroys people, it destroys families, it destroys churches. Sin grieves God and brings his displeasure upon the sinner, and sin is so awful and so serious that it took God in the flesh, dying on the cross of Calvary, to eliminate the eternal consequences of sin for God's people.

Yet in his wisdom and sovereignty, God chose not to eliminate the temporal struggles and consequences of sin in the lives of his people. I get asked often the question: why didn't God just eliminate everything and take sin away and make life easier? Why do we have to struggle with this? There are some answers to that, but the ultimate answer is that somehow for you and me to grow in our sanctification through the struggles of life brings more glory to God and is better for us than if he had just automatically made us all sanctified.

Why? How do we know that? Because the Bible says, "God, you are good and you do good." And if that's what he's doing, then that is what is good.

## The Reality of Struggle with Sin in the Christian Life

As Christians, our lives are at times marked by what seems to be a constant struggle with sin. It's not all the time, it's not every season, but there are seasons of the Christian life where it feels like there's not an ounce of grace. It feels like we pray and our prayers hit the ceiling and don't get past that. We read the Bible and it doesn't seem like we are gaining anything. We come to church and we don't experience the presence of the Lord. The struggle with sin is more real. It's powerful and we feel at times like we can't do anything because sin has that control over us.

If you ever found yourself in that situation, let me tell you of somebody else who found himself in that situation: the Apostle Paul.

### Paul's Struggle with Sin

In Romans chapter 7 verses 18 through 24, Paul says:

> For I know that in me that is in my flesh nothing good dwells. For to will is present with me, but how to perform what is good I do not find. For the good that I will to do I do not do, but the evil I will not to do that I practice. Now if I do what I will not to do, there's no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me. I find then a law that the evil is present with me, the one who wills to do good. For I delight in the law of God according to the inward man, but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin, which is in my members. O wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death? (Romans 7:18-24)

Paul is not just making a theological statement here, though he is. This is how it feels. When you look at yourself at times, you just can't see anything good there.

At times I myself find the struggle with sin so powerful and so tiring that I just want to give up. At times I'm overwhelmed by the feeling that there isn't one ounce of grace in my body with which to please the Lord. The feeling that no matter what I cannot measure up to what God requires of me. Sometimes God seems to be just this tyrant in heaven who keeps demanding things of me that I can't do. Sometimes, not often, but sometimes the overwhelming sensation comes upon me that it would be better to follow Job's wife's advice and to just curse God and die.

Yet all of these thoughts, all of these ideas, all these emotions come from making God in our own image and expecting him to behave like we do.

### The Answer: Christ Alone

Paul ends his discourse in Romans 7 about his own struggle with sin with the only thought that can take us from the bottom of the pit of despair and set our minds right. When he asks, "O wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" the next thing he says is:

> I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

That's what we need: to go to who Jesus is and what he is. It is Christ and Christ alone who delivers us from sin and who pleases God.

The psalmist recognizes that it is not in him to please God in this psalm. So he throws himself recklessly, as it were, upon the mercy of God. Brothers and sisters and friends, that's the only thing we can do: to throw ourselves with abandonment, recklessly as it were, upon the mercies of God, and we're never going to be disappointed in that.

## Understanding Psalm 6: David's Prayer for Mercy in Chastening

### The Superscription and Musical Setting

If you look at the title of the psalm, it says:

> To the chief musician with stringed instruments on an eight stringed harp, a psalm of David.

This psalm is a song to be sung in the worship of God. It's prescribed to be accompanied by stringed instruments. It is directed to the chief musician, and our pulpit versions translate one word there as "eight stringed instruments." Some of your translations say "according to Sheminith," which more than being an eight stringed instrument, this is more likely the word for octave. There are many musical notations in psalms that nobody knows what they mean, but there are some good guesses. This one would be octave, which means this psalm is designed to be sung by bass voices—a voice that's an octave below the usual—which matches the sorrowful tone of the psalm itself.

### The Occasion and Theme

This was written by David, but it's impossible to figure out when it was written or what occasioned it. Some scholars think it may be related to sins recorded in Scripture, such as the incidents with Bathsheba and Uriah. However, David lived a long enough life that there would be other sins he committed that are not recorded for us in the Old Testament historical books. So when and why this was written, we don't know. But it is a prayer for God's grace in the midst of sin and a prayer for God's grace in the midst of the chastisement, the disciplining of the Lord, because of sin that he had committed.

### Sin, Discipline, and Mercy in Verses 1-3

We see that in verses one through three, where David cries out:

> O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor chasten me in your hot displeasure. Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak. O Lord, heal me, for my bones are troubled. My soul also is greatly troubled, but you, O Lord, how long?

Although sin is not explicitly mentioned in this psalm, it becomes evident that David is asking for God's mercy as God deals with his sin. When we compare this psalm, these first three verses, to the first three verses of Psalm 38, where David is clearly talking about sin:

> O Lord, do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor chasten me in your hot displeasure. For your arrows pierce me deeply and your hand presses me down. There is no soundness in my flesh because of your anger, nor any health in my bones because of my sin. (Psalm 38:1-3)

As we read Psalm 6, it sounds like David is talking about being healed from a sickness. But he's actually talking about sin. So we must understand the language of pain, the language of healing, metaphorically, in referring to sin.

What we know here is that David had sinned and experienced the Lord's discipline because of his sin, which discipline was intended to drive David to repentance.

### Discipline vs. Punishment

Let me stop here, brother and sister. If you're in Christ, God doesn't punish you. What's the difference? Punishment is an end in itself. For example, in criminal law, if you murder somebody, you go to jail. Well, in theory, you go to jail forever—it's a life sentence. It's not trying to rehabilitate you. It's not trying to change you. The punishment is the end.

Brothers and sisters, to us who are in Christ, God doesn't do that. He disciplines us. Whatever he brings into our lives as a result of our own sins is to shape us. It's a means to a greater end, and the greater end is repentance and being conformed to the image of Jesus Christ.

So David has sinned and experienced the Lord's discipline, which was intended to drive him to repentance. And notice here that David doesn't ask God not to bring upon him the consequences or the chastisement for his sin. Rather, he asks God to do so in mercy. Yes, Lord, bring the discipline. Yes, Lord, chasten me. Yes, Lord, shape me to be more like Christ. It's going to be hard and it's going to be difficult. But I want that to be accompanied by your mercy, not your anger.

It's not the rebuke that David is asking God to remove. It's not the chastening that David wants God to withdraw. What David wants removed is God's anger. He doesn't want to be disciplined in anger. There are two reasons why David prays this prayer:

### Two Reasons for David's Prayer

First, he knows that God chastens those whom he loves. Therefore, the absence of chastening, the absence of disciplining in the hands of God, would show that God didn't care about David. If God let David just go along with his sin, never do anything about it, just let him live in sin and never interfered, that would have meant that God did not love David. David could not bear that thought. That's why he doesn't ask, "Remove the discipline from me," but rather, "Don't do that in wrath."

We read in our responsive reading this morning, in Hebrews chapter 12, that the Lord chastens those whom he loves. This is a quote from Proverbs chapter 3. It's interesting that Hebrews 12 quotes the writings of David's son Solomon. I wonder if that was something that David ingrained in his children as he taught them that the chastening of the Lord is good, that it comes from his love. Solomon, in scripture ratified by the inspiration of Holy Spirit, gives us that in the book of Proverbs.

Now being chastened by the Lord is not pleasant to be sure. I'm not saying go home and pray, "Lord, just discipline me because I want to feel it." That's not what I'm saying. But not being chastened is much less pleasant in the eternal scheme of things, because God allows you to just remain in your sin. That's where you're going to stay for all eternity—separated from him.

Brothers and sisters, the wrath of God is reserved for those who do not belong to him. David understood that if God dealt with him in wrath, David would be outside of God's people. So David says, "Yes, Lord, discipline me, but do that according to your mercy, not according to your wrath."

### David's Appeal Based on God's Character

Notice also that David's prayer for grace and mercy is based on God's character, not on David's. In verse two, he says:

> Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak. O Lord, heal me for my bones are troubled.

He pleads for God's mercy, which is an acknowledgement that he does not deserve anything good that comes from God. The word translated "have mercy" here means "deal graciously with me." So David asks for what he doesn't deserve. He understands that he deserves God's wrath. He says, "Don't deal with me according to what I deserve." And brothers and sisters, we often come before God more like the Pharisee in the parable than the tax collector, where we say, "O God, I thank you so much that you made me such a great person. I'm not like these other people over here. I fast twice a week. I give tithes of all my possessions. Lord, I just thank you that I am who I am."

No, David comes empty handed and says, "Lord, I know that it is your wrath that I deserve, but I know who you are. You're God of grace and mercy. You're God of covenant. Deal with me according to your grace and your mercy." And this is further evidenced by what he says about himself. David says that he was weak and sickly. He doesn't come before God demanding that God forgive him because of how good and deserving he is. It's exactly the opposite.

### The Anguish of Potential Separation from God

Also notice how David cannot bear the fact that God may be dealing with him in wrath. In verse three, he says:

> My soul also is greatly troubled by you, Lord, how long?

His soul is greatly troubled with the prospect of God being displeased with him in the same way he is displeased with his enemies. He asks how long this is going to last.

Brothers and sisters, being in sin annihilates any confidence and assurance that God is our God. I often talk to people and they struggle with their assurance, and then we start talking about what's going on in their lives and they're living in sin. At that point, I just proceed to tell them, "Yeah, you have no reason to be assured of your salvation if that's how you choose to live."

David is greatly troubled about it and we should be as well. In 1st John chapter two, verses three through six, the apostle says:

> Now by this we know that we know him. If we keep his commandments, he who says I know him and does not keep his commandments is a liar and the truth is not in him. But whatever keeps his word, truly the love of God is perfected in him. By this we know that we are in him. He who says he abides in him ought himself also to walk just as he walked.

David's question—"how long"—relates to God's displeasure with his sin. How long, Lord, would you be displeased with my sin? But we often ask it about other areas of life as well, don't we?

## The Question "How Long": Different Contexts

It's okay to ask God how long. It's okay to ask God why. David does that. We might ask God, "How long, Lord, will you make me stay in this awful marriage? How long, Lord, will you be distant from me? How long, Lord, will you let my children rebel? How long, Lord, will you make me go through life alone? How long, how long, how long?"

I think the words of another Psalm are often our words. In Psalm 13, David says:

> How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me? How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? How long will my enemy be exalted over me?

Do you know what the answer is? The answer is always: as long as it takes. As long as it takes for you to be driven to Jesus Christ.

### Lesson One: God Never Forgets His People

There are two vital lessons to remember at a time like this. Regardless of what's going on in your life, if you follow Jesus Christ, God never forgets his people. Therefore, he has not forgotten you.

In Isaiah 49 verses 14 and 15, the people of God say:

> The Lord has forsaken me and my Lord has forgotten me.

That's the accusation against God. And then God replies to them and asks:

> Can a woman forget her nursing child and not have compassion on the son of her womb? How absurd is the idea that a mother would forsake their children? That's foreign to most of our experiences. We think this—it can't be. And yet sometimes it happens. Surely they may forget, yet I will not forget you.

Your human relationships might fail you. The closest of those familial relationships—a mother and a child—might be broken. But I, the Lord, will never forget you.

And you may suffer for years, but that is not because God forgets you, for he says:

> I will never leave you nor forsake you.

As I say this, you may push back. You might say, "But God does seemingly forget some of his chosen. Look at Joseph. Joseph served the Lord and every time he did, he got hit in the head and put into jail. He tried to be faithful to the Lord. He ends up in a pit, sold into slavery. He is faithful over Potiphar's household. He obeys the Lord. He refuses sexual immorality. And what is the result? Put in jail. He's faithful in jail. He becomes the chief prisoner of the jail. The Lord gives him the content of the dreams of the cupbearer and the baker. It comes to pass and they forget Joseph. So he lingers in jail for about two years. But eventually the Lord brought him back and restored him.

David himself was a man that seemed forgotten by the Lord. Paul—all of them were shut up in unpleasant circumstances for years during which it seemed that God had forgotten them.

How do you deal with that? Well, do you know what was happening during that time? Do you know what was happening in those years of Joseph or of David or of Paul? God was building maturity in those men as they learned to trust in him. Just as it takes years to grow a mighty oak, so it takes years to build the godly character qualities needed to be an effective servant of the Lord.

### Lesson Two: There Is No Instant Godliness

This brings us to another lesson: there's no such thing as instant godliness. David was anointed as king in his teens—as early as sixteen, somewhere between sixteen and eighteen. He had a strong faith at the time. You remember the whole battle with Goliath? He arrived at camp to bring some food to the brothers and to the king, and he hears this giant defying the God of Israel, saying, "This god is nothing. Nobody's willing to come out and say, 'Why are you all standing here when he's defaming our God?'" And he goes on and by faith with just a stone—five stones, he only needed one—and a slingshot, he kills the one that nobody thought could be killed. Didn't he become the king of Israel? In fact, right then, was the throne his? Was it when he turned twenty-one? Or twenty-five? Or twenty-seven? Or twenty-nine? No. He kept on just being chased around by Saul in the wilderness, living in caves for over ten years. "Lord, did you forget me? Did you forget me?"

In 1 Samuel 16, God crowned him king—God anointed him king—and yet all he did was live in caves. No, the Lord was preparing his people. There's no such thing as instant godliness. That's so out of sync with our always-in-a-hurry world, but that's how God works.

Paul is saved on the road to Damascus. Paul would have the equivalent of a PhD in Jewish scripture. He would know the Old Testament—which was the Bible of the time—better than anybody. He gets saved, hits the floor, is baptized by Ananias, and then what? Wait. Three years. I wonder if that's why seminaries are three years long. But three years. And that's the guy who was an expert. And yet three years he goes to the wilderness and studies. "Get to know me. Even though you have a doctorate in theology, go get to know me."

If God has placed you in some frustrating circumstances and he seems far away, hang on. Let God do his perfect work in you. He hasn't forgotten you. He's just teaching you to wait. Do you know what's the most prevalent command, the most common commandment in the book of Psalms? Wait. Wait. But it's an act of wait. It's a waiting on the Lord. It's waiting by faith in him, by growing in him.

## David's Prayer of Deliverance: Verses 4-7

That's what led David to pray the prayer in verses four through seven, a prayer of deliverance. In verse four, he says:

> Return, O Lord, deliver me, O save me for your mercy's sake.

David is so troubled that he asks God just to save him. There's nothing he can do. He arrived at the end of his rope. He just can't turn to God. And sometimes that's what God is doing in our lives. He's getting us to the point where we arrive at the place where we know that there's nothing else we can do. We've tried everything. We failed. Our best efforts didn't work. We were cast out. And yet we're still here. And then we turn to the Lord. There was a guy that used to say that Jesus's office was at the end of your rope.

It's true. Jesus lives at the end of our ropes. When we get there, then we're ready for Jesus to work in us.

One important thing for us to notice here is that David keeps on reminding God of his covenant faithfulness. In these four verses, five times, David calls God by his covenant name Yahweh, the Lord who is, the one who is and always will be. He pleads with God to save him as a display of his covenantal love. The word translated "mercies" is the word for "loving kindness" or "steadfast love," and it finds its origins in God's covenant grace with his elect.

David asks God to look at himself, to look at God himself. Lord, look at you. Not me. Your mercy is based on you, on yourself. So don't just look at me to act towards me. Look at yourself to find the mercy and the grace to deal with my situation.

David really understands the seriousness of his sin and how devastating it would be if God didn't forgive him. In verses six and seven, he says:

> I am weary with my groaning. All night I make my bed swim. I drench my couch with my tears. My eye wastes away because of grief. It grows old because of all my enemies.

It's big, dramatic, right? Maybe he's one of those kids that dramaticized everything. But here he says he cried so much that he's super tired. He has cried so much that his bed is floating on his tears. That's the idea. He's cried to the point that his eyes are so swollen that he can't see anything. What is he crying over? The fact that he sinned against his God.

## The Most Difficult Verse: Psalm 6:5

And that brings us to the most difficult verse in Psalm 6, which is verse five:

> For in death there is no remembrance of you, in the grave, who will give you thanks?

When you get to a complicated verse like this, you try to research and look at all the commentaries and look at five commentaries to see what they said about this verse. After looking at five commentaries, each one gave me a different way of interpreting this verse. So after a lot of study, I came up with five different ways to interpret it, and none of them seemed right. So I came up with a sixth one.

I think that David was really in doubt whether he was going to heaven. The word translated "grave" could also be translated "hell." This would show that he had been so caught up in his sin that there was no assurance of salvation left in his soul. So he brings up the possibility of going to hell or the place of the dead. And that's something that's important for us to remember, brothers and sisters.

Dying is only gain. Remember Philippians 1:21? Dying is only gain if living is what? Christ. When living is not Christ, there's no confidence that dying will be gain.

I believe that this is the predicament that David found himself in. His sin had so damaged his assurance that he was unable to rest in the promise of eternal life.

## David's Deliverance: Verses 8-10

And yet the Lord in his goodness and mercy answered his prayer. And we find that in verses eight through ten. David says:

> Depart from me all you workers of iniquity for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.

The feeling we get here is that David was sinning with other people—that he was going along with the wicked. And now that the Lord has answered his prayer, he says, "I'm going to part with the wicked." There's a sudden change in the mood of the Psalm here, which led some scholars to think that these verses were written at a different time by a different person. However, the change of mood can be easily accounted for by God's answering David's prayer.

In verse eight, he says:

> Depart from you all you workers of iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping. The Lord has heard my supplication. The Lord will receive my prayers.

Then he makes this prayer:

> Let all the enemies be ashamed and greatly troubled, let them turn back and be ashamed suddenly.

If it is meant to be a statement, David is praying that his enemies—the wicked that with whom he was sinning—would go through the same chastisement that he had gone through so that they can repent. That's what David would be praying for: the repentance of the wicked.

Though there's nothing in the grammar of the text that requires one way or another, I think that contextually David is praying for his enemies. David is praying for the salvation of his people just like we have in the New King James.

He has gone through it and he's seen the benefit—that all those trials, all those struggles, all those chastisements, all that discipline from the Lord caused him to love God more and to see God more clearly. And he said, "I want the same for those people I was sinning with. I want them to come to see Jesus. I want them to come to salvation. I want them to come to repentance. I want them to come to greater faith in Christ. I want them to come to a life that is full of God's joy."

What a great way to end the psalm—praying for the repentance of those who claim to be God's people, right? Because these will be people in Israel and yet live as if they are not.

## Living Out Psalm 6 in Light of the Gospel

So how do we live out what this psalm teaches in light of the gospel? We leave here after the afternoon service today and then hit real life as it were. How are we going to live this out?

### First: Run to Christ When Your Sin Condemns You

First, run to Christ when your sin condemns you. Don't stay there. Run to Christ. We saw that David's greatest fear was not the pain of discipline, but the possibility of being under God's wrath.

The gospel tells us that what David longed for has been fully accomplished in Christ. What David believed in and saw at a distance we know fully: that Christ died for our sins. Jesus endured the wrath that our sins deserve so that God's children would never experience his judicial condemnation.

So when your conscience accuses you and Satan reminds you of your failures, do not look within yourself for assurance. All you're going to see in there is darkness. You need to look to Christ. The Father no longer deals with believers as condemned criminals, but as beloved sons and daughters.

Remember what John says in 1 John 3: "What manner of love the Father has bestowed upon us is given to us that we might be called children of God."

His discipline is now fatherly, not judicial, because Christ has already borne the curse in our place. So learn from David. Run to Christ.

### Second: Bring Your Deepest Sorrow to Jesus

Secondly, bring your deepest sorrow to Jesus because he understands repentant sinners. It's okay to come to God with a humble heart and ask how long or why. David flooded his bed with his tears and the Lord heard every cry.

And the gospel reveals an even greater comfort. The Savior to whom we pray is the man of sorrows who himself wept, agonized in Gethsemane, and cried out on the cross. He's not indifferent to the broken hearted sinners who come in repentance.

No matter how deep your guilt, how long your struggle with sin has lasted or how distant God may seem, Christ invites weary sinners to come to him. He does not cast out those who confess their sins and seek his mercy, because he ever lives to intercede for his people.

We can approach the throne of grace with confidence. If you have not come before Christ for a while, if you're afraid that he might reject you, don't fear. If the Father has given you to him, he'll take you and he'll never cast you out.

### Third: Wait Patiently for God's Sanctifying Work

And lastly, wait patiently for God's sanctifying work because Christ is committed to finish what he began. David throughout the Psalms repeatedly cried out, "How long?" And every Christian knows that question. Every Christian has asked that question. We long for victory over sin, relief from suffering. We long for greater holiness, yet God's work often seems painfully slow.

The gospel reminds us that our standing with God rests not on the speed of our sanctification, but on the finished work of Christ. It's not how holy you are. It is what Christ has done for you.

The same Savior who justified you is also sanctifying you. And God often uses seasons of conviction, discipline, and waiting to make us more like his Son.

So, brothers and sisters, don't lose heart when growth seems slow. Christ has promised to complete the good work he began in his people. And one day, the struggle with sin will end forever when we're glorified in his presence. He who began a good work in you will complete it.
